newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Main events in road to Swiss Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Main events in road to Swiss Holocaust fund.

text.p: Chronology of main events leading up to the formal creation of a Holocaust memorial fund by the Swiss government on Wednesday:
1995 - Foreign and domestic criticism grows of Swiss banks' handling of dormant accounts of Holocaust victims and the country's purchases of looted gold from Nazi Germany during World War Two
March 27, 1995 - Member of Parliament Verena Grendelmeier launches initiative with goal of government decree on tracking down and returning dormant wealth

September 8, 1995 - Swiss Bankers Association issues new guidelines on how members should handle dormant accounts, agrees to set up ombudsman who will coordinate requests for information from potential claimants
February 7, 1996 - Ombudsman's survey finds around 38.7 million Swiss francs in unclaimed wealth in bank accounts opened before 1945. World Jewish Congress estimates the amount is much higher
April 23, 1996 - U.S. Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato starts hearings on Swiss banks' handling of dormant accounts

May 2, 1996 - Swiss bankers and Jewish groups agree to create independent panel to search for any unclaimed wealth at Swiss banks. Former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker named head of the panel in August
September 30, 1996 - Lower house of parliament approves federal decree calling for probe of Swiss role as financial centre during World War Two

October 3, 1996 - Auschwitz survivor Gizella Weisshaus files class-action suit in New York against two big Swiss banks asking $20 billion for Nazi victims. Five other survivors file a separate suit against Swiss banks on October 23

October 16, 1996 - Senator D'Amato cites U.S. archival material to allege Swiss used dormant wealth of Polish Jews to compensate Swiss citizens for property nationalised by Warsaw's post-war communist regime under 1949 treaty
October 23, 1996 - Swiss foreign ministry asks two historians to probe D'Amato's allegations, creates task force to coordinate Swiss response to rising tide of critics' accusations

November 12, 1996 - After one-year search, banks' ombudsman says he has matched 1.6 million francs in dormant wealth to 11 rightful owners, but found only 11,000 francs owned by people persecuted by the Nazis
November 18, 1996 - British MPs Greville Janner and Sir David Hunt call in Berne for quick creation of a fund to compensate recognised victims of the Nazis
November 27, 1996 - Some Holocaust survivors call for boycott of Swiss banks in effort to prompt gesture to Hitler's victims

December 11, 1996 - Task force chief Thomas Borer tells U.S. House of Representatives Banking Committee that Switzerland will quickly compile report on its wartime role; World Jewish Congress (WJC) President Edgar Bronfman and D'Amato seeks financaial gesture from Switzerland as a sign of good will

December 13, 1996 - Parliament gives final approval to decree on sweeping historical probe of wartime era; Swiss National Bank says its earned around 20 million francs through wartime gold transactions with Nazis
December 19, 1996 - Government names nine-member international panel of historians to probe wartime era

December 31, 1996 - Economics Minister and outgoing President Jean-Pascal Delamuraz likens Jewish calls for restitution to "extortion and blackmail" in newspaper interview, touching off protests and renewed threats of a boycott call

January 7, 1997 - Swiss government calls for immediate talks with banks and Jewish groups on using dormant accounts to create Holocaust memorial fund, leaves open door for adding public money as a gesture of good will

January 14, 1997 - Private security guard at Union Bank of Switzerland reveals he removed old documents bound for shreder at the bank and turned them over the Swiss Jewish leaders; UBS calls it shredding "regrettable mistake"
January 15, 1997 - Delamuraz apologises for blackmail remark
January 22, 1997 - Credit Suisse Chairman Rainer Gut proposes that government, Swiss National Bank and private banks and insurers create humanitarian fund for Nazi victims and their relatives
January 23, 1997 - Government welcomes Gut's call and says it will discuss creating fund with banks; officials agree in principle to proceed with fund during talks with senior business executives
January 26, 1997 - Newspaper publishes leaked document in which Swiss ambassador to Washington calls for "waging war" against Jewish groups and other vocal critics, prompting envoy's resignation
January 29, 1997 - New York city and state warn Switzerland they can make it tough for Swiss banks to do business there unless Swiss set up fund for Holocaust victims
February 5, 1997 - Three biggest Swiss banks contribute 100 million Swiss francs to humanitarian fund for Holocaust victims; other businesses pledge to follow suit
February 6, 1997 - Jewish leaders drop plans for Swiss bank boycott
February 12, 1997 - Swiss government agrees to create immediately a memorial fund that taps contributions from banks and other businesses to aid Holocaust victims
February 26, 1997 - Government gives final approval to fund after working out administrative details with Jewish groups
